subject: Exhibit B request: operational separation & split-control key model for private deployment

Subject: Request: DPA exhibit — operational separation for on-prem deployment

David / Karthik,

Thanks for the private deployment overview last week. As part of our internal review we need an explicit Exhibit to the DPA that covers operational separation, key control, and subprocessors for the on-prem/VPC installation model you're proposing.

Key asks we need captured in the Exhibit:
- Clear statement that customer retains sole control over cryptographic keys (including support for customer KMS/HSM).
- Description of the runtime key usage model (ephemeral vs persistent keys) and whether Redwood can unwrap or export keys.
- List of Redwood subprocessors that will have any network-level or operational visibility into the deployed environment (e.g., monitoring, logging, patching).
- Operator access model and break-glass procedures (including who, for what reasons, and what logging is created).
- Data egress guarantees (models, KV cache, request/response artifacts) and telemetry minimization.
- Cross-border transfer restrictions / region pinning language for workloads that must remain within the US.

I've attached a short requirements brief (exhibit-b-reqs.pdf) for your counsel and engineering team to review. Can you confirm whether you can accept these items as an Exhibit to the DPA, and if not, which items are negotiable? We'd like to close the legal review by EOD June 18 if possible.

Thanks,
Asha Reddy
Sr. Counsel, HealthBridge Medical
asha.reddy@healthbridge.com

Asha,

Appreciate the clear asks and the brief. We can take these on and have put together a first-pass Exhibit for your review (attached: redwood-prop-exhibitB-draft.pdf). High level: we propose a split-control key model that keeps the unwrapped key material under customer control while allowing the runtime to operate with short-lived wrapping tokens — in practice this prevents Redwood personnel from accessing plaintext keys or unwrapped symmetric keys used to encrypt inference state.

Quick summary of the draft and open questions:
- Key control: customer KMS/HSM holds key-encryption keys; Redwood receives short-lived, purpose-limited wrapped keys for runtime use. No plaintext master keys are exported.
- Operator access: Redwood engineers can only access node-level consoles through customer-initiated break-glass; access must be approved by the customer, time-limited, and streamed to your audit collection.
- Subprocessors: initial list in the draft includes our managed OS image vendor and monitoring provider; we call out scope (IP-level, not decrypted payloads) and invite any additional vendor checks.
- Data egress: exhibit states no model weights or KV caches will be exported by Redwood; diagnostic bundles are sanitized by a telemetry scrubbing step before leaving the environment.
- Region pinning: we include an option to bind inference traffic to a specific cloud region and to prevent replication outside that region.

Action items:
1) Would you be open to a 30-minute call Monday to walk through the draft (we can bring a brief network diagram)?
2) Please flag any non-starters in the draft; the doc currently lists a couple of alternate wordings for "operator access" that we can tighten with legal.

I've attached a VPC access map (vpc-access-map.png) and the Exhibit draft. If that looks reasonable, we'll ask engineering to produce a short technical appendix for the security team.

Best,
David Kim
Head of Strategic Accounts, Redwood Inference

On Mon, Jun 16, 2025 at 9:07 AM David Kim <david.kim@redwoodinference.com> wrote:
> I've attached a VPC access map (vpc-access-map.png) and the Exhibit draft.

Hi Asha / team,

Following up with a technical appendix so your security folks can evaluate the feasibility of the proposed wording. The core of our approach is a "split-control" runtime pattern (summary below). I've attached a short tech appendix (tech-appendix-split-key.txt).

Technical summary (plain language):
- Key wrapping: Customer KMS holds the KEK (key-encryption key). During model boot the customer grants a short-lived wrapping token signed by their KMS. The runtime receives wrapped DEKs (data encryption keys) for in-memory use only.
- No persistent unwrapped keys: DEKs are unwrapped in-memory on the node and evicted from RAM after session end; nothing is persisted in plaintext on disk.
- Operator tooling: Redwood's operator tooling can request diagnostics; those bundles are created by a local agent which redacts user identifiers and obfuscates request payloads by default. Only with customer approval would more detailed logs be exported.
- Audit & telemetry: We stream audit events (authentication, operator sessions, config changes) to an append-only audit log within your VPC. Redwood maintains a copy of metadata (no PII) for billing and support, unless you elect an option to disable remote metadata retention.
- Subprocessor visibility: We will include the subprocessors list nominated in the Exhibit; any subprocessors with potential network reach into the environment are subject to your security review.

Suggested DPA clause tweak: replace the generic "reasonable access" language with specific steps for break-glass (approval workflow, ticket id, session recording retention). That makes operational expectations auditable.

If acceptable, engineering can produce an explicit sequence diagram and memory lifecycle notes for inclusion as a technical annex.

-Karthik
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
